projects.name: LLM-ProS
projects.title: What can a model solve on its first try?
projects.summary: A zero-shot evaluation of five LLMs on 166 ICPC World Finals problems, using official judge verdicts to examine correctness, error patterns, and temporal performance.
projects.pitch: LLM-ProS benchmarks five models on 166 ICPC World Finals problems in a single-attempt setting. I built the problem collection and submission pipeline and analyzed correctness and failure patterns. The reasoning-oriented o1 models solved 16 and 15 problems; the other three solved none in this setting. The study motivated moving from measuring one-shot capability to testing how execution feedback can help.
ownership: Automated collection and preprocessing of 166 ICPC problems.
Built Codeforces Gym submission and verdict collection.
Analyzed correctness, error types, runtime and memory evidence.
projects.finding: o1-mini: 9.64%; o1-preview: 9.04%. GPT-4o, Mistral Large and Llama-3.1-405B: 0 accepted under this protocol.
projects.caution: Model-family comparisons do not isolate chain-of-thought as a causal factor. Year-based results suggest contamination risk; they do not prove which examples were in training.
projects.next: A-ProS adds repeated execution feedback to this evaluation setting.

projects.name: A-ProS
projects.title: Can useful feedback improve the next attempt?
projects.summary: A generator and a debugging critic work through judge feedback, with persistent conversation context and up to three refinement rounds. Six model pairings are evaluated on 367 problems.
projects.pitch: A-ProS separates writing a solution from diagnosing its failures. We evaluated two generators paired with three critics, on 167 ICPC and 200 Codeforces problems. I built orchestration, submission, verdict logging and the ablation and calibration analyses. On ICPC, GPT-5 workflows went from 39 accepted solutions to 85 to 90 after three refinement rounds. A 47-problem memory ablation showed less verdict repetition, but its solve-rate differences were not statistically conclusive.
ownership: Designed orchestration and implemented Selenium/Playwright automation.
Built verdict capture and SQLite experiment logging.
Conducted context-memory ablations and critic calibration analysis.
projects.finding: Stateful refinement had a descriptive 8.5 to 10.6 percentage-point advantage on 47 matched problems, and 2.9 to 3.5 times lower verdict repetition.
projects.caution: 39 to 90 is out of 167 ICPC problems, not all 367. Memory solve-rate confidence intervals touch zero. More than 2× refers to gains over the initial baseline, not final accuracy.
projects.next: XLAgent moves from isolated contest solutions to defects across repository language boundaries.

projects.name: XLAgent
projects.title: What breaks when two languages meet?
projects.summary: An empirical study and repair framework for Java-TypeScript and Python-Go bugs. It combines a cross-language navigation graph, localization, contract reasoning, editing and isolated evaluation.
projects.pitch: XLAgent studies bugs that require coordinated changes across interacting languages. I carried out the project with Md. Fahim Arefin as PI. We mined 145 repositories, confirmed 86 candidate fixes and retained 31 under a strict definition. The graph connected 11 of 12 in-scope fixes, but did not improve localization over shell search. On five executable bugs, the system edited both developer-file sides more often, but did not establish better repair correctness. The most important lessons concern leakage and the limits of the evaluation oracle.
ownership: Author record: carried out the project independently, with Md. Fahim Arefin as PI.
Built mining, graph navigation, localization/editing and evaluation infrastructure.
Investigated leakage, test coupling, matched controls and narrowed claims.
projects.finding: Developer-file two-sided edits: 4.0 / 5 versus 2.7 for baseline and 3.0 for a matched single agent, averaged across three replicates. Repair correctness did not improve.
projects.caution: Only Python-Go bugs are executable in the repair set. Three of five hidden suites depend on developer-specific names. Graph localization results are null. Manuscript remains in preparation.
projects.next: A PhD direction: reliable evidence and behavioral oracles for agentic software repair.

questions.question: What is LLM-ProS in 30 seconds?
questions.answer: It is a zero-shot benchmarking framework for five LLMs on 166 ICPC World Finals problems. We submit generated solutions to Codeforces Gym and analyze acceptance and failure verdicts.
detail: Explain the task, the automated pipeline, the main result, then why it led to feedback-based work.
o1-mini solved 16 problems and o1-preview solved 15; the other tested models solved none under this protocol.
questions.caution: This is a workshop publication at ICSE 2025 LLM4Code.
followups: Why ICPC?
What did you personally build?

questions.question: What research question did LLM-ProS address?
questions.answer: We asked how well contemporary LLMs solve difficult algorithmic problems on the first attempt, how performance varies by year and topic, and what failure patterns appear.
detail: The four questions concern temporal generalization, categories, variation across model families, and verdict distributions.
A judge provides more concrete evidence than judging whether generated source looks plausible.
questions.caution: The design compares existing systems; it does not identify their hidden training mechanisms.
followups: What does acceptance actually measure?

questions.question: Why use ICPC World Finals problems?
questions.answer: They require choosing an algorithm, implementing it correctly, handling edge cases and meeting time and memory limits. That makes them a demanding controlled test of program generation.
detail: Problems include explicit specifications and an established execution oracle.
Their difficulty exposes failures that easier code-completion tasks can hide.
questions.caution: Contest tasks represent a narrow part of software engineering. They do not measure repository maintenance or collaboration.
followups: How would you evaluate repository work instead?

questions.question: Which models and problems were evaluated?
questions.answer: Five models: GPT-4o, Mistral Large, Llama-3.1-405B, o1-mini and o1-preview. The benchmark contains 166 ICPC World Finals problems from 2011 through 2024.
detail: State the exact model versions used in the paper, rather than substituting newer models.
Each problem gets a first-attempt generated solution evaluated by the judge.
questions.caution: These are historical model results, not a current leaderboard.
followups: Why not compare only models with equal compute?

questions.question: What were the headline results?
questions.answer: o1-mini obtained 16 accepted solutions out of 166, or 9.64%; o1-preview obtained 15, or 9.04%. GPT-4o, Mistral Large and Llama-3.1-405B obtained zero accepted solutions in this setting.
detail: The absolute counts matter because even the best model solved a small fraction.
Mention both the separation between model families and the remaining difficulty.
questions.caution: Zero acceptance here does not mean those models cannot write useful code in general.
followups: Does the ranking establish a causal explanation?

questions.question: What is your contribution to LLM-ProS?
questions.answer: I designed the automated problem collection and preprocessing pipeline, built Codeforces Gym submission automation, and analyzed correctness and execution results.
detail: Describe an artifact you can explain end to end: source statement, cleaned prompt, generated solution, submission identifier, verdict and analysis.
Credit the coauthors for the joint research rather than claiming sole ownership.
questions.caution: Personal responsibilities follow the author profile; author order alone would not establish them.
followups: What part was hardest?
How did you validate preprocessing?

questions.question: Walk me through the pipeline.
questions.answer: Collect ICPC statements, extract and validate their components, format prompts, request a model solution, submit to Codeforces Gym, and store verdicts for analysis.
detail: Preserve constraints, input/output formats, examples and mathematical notation.
Separate API or submission failures from generated-program failures so infrastructure does not silently become a model error.
questions.caution: The latter separation is an evaluation practice to check in logs, not an extra reported result.
followups: Where could the pipeline introduce bias?

questions.question: How did you preprocess problem statements?
questions.answer: We extracted statements, input and output specifications, examples, notes and limits, then cleaned encoding and formatting and manually checked the resulting prompts.
detail: PDF extraction can lose superscripts, inequalities, tables or geometry diagrams.
Validate a sample against the original and preserve any information needed to solve the problem.
questions.caution: A clean-looking prompt can still be semantically incomplete.
followups: How would you test extraction quality?

questions.question: What does zero-shot mean in this study?
questions.answer: The model receives the problem specification without worked training examples for that task and generates its first solution without iterative judge feedback.
detail: Public sample input/output is part of the specification.
Zero-shot does not mean the model has never encountered the problem during pretraining.
questions.caution: Distinguish prompt setup from training contamination.
followups: Is zero-shot the same as uncontaminated?

questions.question: What does pass@1 measure here?
questions.answer: The fraction of benchmark problems whose first generated candidate is accepted by the judge under this protocol.
detail: For o1-mini it is 16 divided by 166.
It is a measured first-attempt success rate, distinct from success after several feedback rounds or best-of-k sampling.
questions.caution: Finite tests and harness correctness bound what acceptance establishes.
followups: How is pass@k different?

questions.question: Why use an external judge?
questions.answer: It evaluates programs against a stable task-specific test suite and resource limits, reducing reliance on subjective inspection of source code.
detail: Verdicts distinguish accepted, wrong answer, compile error, runtime error, time limit and memory limit failures.
The judge is evidence of behavior under its tests.
questions.caution: Acceptance is not a proof of correctness for all possible inputs.
followups: What can a judge miss?

questions.question: What can go wrong in browser submission automation?
questions.answer: Authentication, dynamic pages, delayed verdicts, language selection and retries can all corrupt the mapping from candidate to result.
detail: A robust design records problem, candidate hash and submission identifier; waits for a terminal verdict; and avoids duplicating submissions on uncertain retries.
I would demonstrate the actual implementation before claiming every safeguard was present.
questions.caution: This answer separates engineering practices from paper-verified implementation details.
questions.locator: Section IV implementation; proposed engineering checks
followups: How would you make retries idempotent?

questions.question: Were prompts exactly identical across models?
questions.answer: The paper uses standardized problem components with some model-specific template adjustments, including additional reasoning guidance for the o1 family.
detail: This helps compatibility but creates a possible prompt confound in a model-family comparison.
A stronger follow-up would cross models with several matched prompt templates.
questions.caution: Do not describe the comparison as isolating model training alone.
followups: What matched control would you add?

questions.question: What information should be logged for reproducibility?
questions.answer: The exact task, prompt, model identifier, configuration, generated source, submission identifier and verdict should be retained.
detail: Include timestamps and raw failures, not just summary tables.
API aliases and judge behavior can change, so version evidence and immutable artifacts are useful.
questions.caution: This is a reproducibility checklist; it does not assert every item was preserved in every historical run.
followups: How do you handle changing model endpoints?

questions.question: Does this prove chain-of-thought caused the better performance?
questions.answer: No. The reasoning-oriented model families performed better, but architecture, training data, compute and prompt differences were not independently controlled.
detail: Describe the observed association and the authors' interpretation separately.
A causal test would need controlled interventions or much more closely matched models and budgets.
questions.caution: Avoid saying the study isolated chain-of-thought as the primary cause.
followups: What experiment could isolate the effect?

questions.question: Did you prove dataset contamination?
questions.answer: No. Temporal performance patterns raise a contamination concern, but a year-based split cannot reveal the contents of proprietary training data.
detail: Older and newer problems also differ in difficulty and sample size.
Say potentially exposed older problems and temporally held-out 2024 problems under the stated cutoff assumptions.
questions.caution: Do not call the benchmark proven contamination-free.
followups: What stronger contamination audit is possible?

questions.question: What happened on the 2024 problems?
questions.answer: The paper reports 15.4% acceptance for o1-mini and 7.7% for o1-preview on the 2024 subset.
detail: The subset is small, so a difference of one accepted problem changes the percentage substantially.
Explain why counts and uncertainty are helpful alongside percentages.
questions.caution: Do not generalize one year into a stable population ranking.
followups: How would you report confidence intervals?

questions.question: Why did three models score zero?
questions.answer: The data show their candidates failed the judge under this demanding first-attempt setup. A breakdown of verdicts helps identify compilation, runtime and semantic failures.
detail: GPT-4o had 41 compile errors and 55 wrong answers in Table II.
Low success could reflect several interacting factors, including prompt compatibility and task difficulty.
questions.caution: A zero count does not identify one underlying cause.
followups: Would feedback help them?

questions.question: What is the dominant o1-mini failure mode?
questions.answer: Wrong Answer: 124 of 166 candidates, compared with 16 accepted, 10 compile errors, 13 time-limit failures and one memory-limit failure.
detail: This suggests syntactically plausible programs can still miss the intended algorithm or edge cases.
A verdict taxonomy is a starting point for semantic inspection.
questions.caution: Wrong Answer is an outcome, not a root-cause label. The paper's o1-mini row sums to 164 despite the 166-task denominator, so its full accounting needs reconciliation.
followups: How would you identify the actual root cause?

questions.question: Are there any table inconsistencies worth acknowledging?
questions.answer: The o1-mini and Llama-3.1 verdict rows in Table II each sum to 164 while the benchmark contains 166 problems. I would reconcile the submission ledger before presenting either row as a complete accounting.
detail: The reported accepted counts remain 16 for o1-mini and zero for Llama-3.1.
Do not invent missing verdicts or infer why these rows are short.
questions.caution: This is a source-table accounting issue, not evidence of what happened to those two cases.
questions.locator: Table II, o1-mini and Llama-3.1 rows
followups: What ledger would resolve the discrepancy?

questions.question: Can you generalize these results to software engineering?
questions.answer: Only cautiously. Contest programs have self-contained specifications and strong judges; maintenance work has dependencies, ambiguous reports, evolving interfaces and multiple files.
detail: LLM-ProS motivates studying those differences rather than establishing repository-level repair performance.
XLAgent is one attempt to investigate that next setting.
questions.caution: Cross-project progression does not make their numerical scores directly comparable.
followups: Why is repository repair harder?

questions.question: How would you improve the study now?
questions.answer: Add budget-matched prompts, multiple independent samples, a stronger temporal protocol, validated extraction and detailed semantic failure labels.
detail: Report uncertainty and counts by year and difficulty, not only averages.
Use a fresh held-out problem stream and archive exact model outputs.
questions.caution: These are proposed extensions, not experiments completed in LLM-ProS.
followups: Which improvement would you prioritize?

questions.question: What did LLM-ProS teach you?
questions.answer: A working evaluation pipeline is a research instrument. A polished-looking solution is weak evidence; judged outcomes reveal failures, and the evaluation itself still needs validation.
detail: This led naturally to asking whether structured execution feedback improves later attempts in A-ProS.
It also prepared me to investigate leakage and oracle limitations in XLAgent.
questions.caution: Present this as a research lesson, not an additional empirical result.
followups: How did this change your next project?

questions.question: What is A-ProS in 30 seconds?
questions.answer: A-ProS is an inference-time programming workflow: a generator writes code, a judge evaluates it, and a separate critic diagnoses failures so the generator can revise with context.
detail: We compare six pairings across 367 problems.
It uses at most one initial attempt plus three refinement rounds and stops early on acceptance.
questions.caution: It does not update model weights during the loop.
followups: How is it different from LLM-ProS?

questions.question: How does A-ProS extend LLM-ProS?
questions.answer: LLM-ProS measures a first attempt. A-ProS studies whether judge evidence, a specialized critic and persistent interaction can improve subsequent attempts.
detail: The research question shifts from capability measurement to workflow design.
Models and task sets differ, so avoid treating their scores as a controlled before-and-after comparison.
questions.caution: This is a conceptual progression, not a matched experiment between papers.
followups: Why separate generator and critic?

questions.question: What did you personally contribute to A-ProS?
questions.answer: I designed the orchestration pipeline, built browser submission and verdict capture, implemented SQLite logging, and conducted persistent-context ablations and calibration analyses.
detail: Give concrete implementation decisions and explain how the stored artifacts supported a research question.
I share equal contribution with Anika Tabassum; this is a joint paper.
questions.caution: Ownership follows the author profile, rather than an inference from the manuscript.
followups: Explain one design choice you made.

questions.question: What is the 2 by 3 factorial design?
questions.answer: Two generators, GPT-4 and GPT-5, are each paired separately with Codestral-2508, Llama-3.3-70B and DeepSeek-R1 as debugging critics, giving six workflows.
detail: One generator and one critic operate in a workflow.
The three critics are alternatives, not a three-model voting panel.
questions.caution: The design lacks a same-model generator-critic control for isolating heterogeneity.
followups: What extra control would you add?

questions.question: Why separate generation from criticism?
questions.answer: The roles have different jobs: synthesis must produce an executable solution, while criticism should diagnose the failure and suggest a targeted revision.
detail: The separation lets us vary critics while keeping a generator fixed.
It makes feedback behavior observable through stored hints and outcomes.
questions.caution: Role separation alone does not prove multi-model superiority.
followups: Could one model do both jobs?

questions.question: What exactly reaches the critic?
questions.answer: The problem specification, failed candidate and available execution diagnostics, such as verdict and accessible failing-test information.
detail: The critic proposes a debugging hint rather than directly submitting the next solution.
The generator remains responsible for implementing the revision.
questions.caution: Detailed hidden-test information is not universally available for all tasks.
followups: How do you avoid leaking hidden evaluation data?

questions.question: What does persistent context preserve?
questions.answer: Earlier conversational turns for the current task, including previous candidates, failures and feedback, within the relevant generator and critic sessions.
detail: It can discourage returning to a failed approach.
Each role can retain its own history; this is not a shared learned memory across unrelated tasks.
questions.caution: Longer histories also consume more tokens and can retain incorrect advice.
followups: Why might a summary be better than full history?

questions.question: What is the stateless ablation?
questions.answer: Before each refinement, prior conversation turns are cleared, but the latest failure verdict and critic hint remain in the current prompt.
detail: The paper compares accumulated history with latest feedback alone.
It does not compare all feedback against no feedback.
questions.caution: Check the historical experiment version before reproducing it with the current local solver, whose mode names differ.
followups: What must be held constant?

questions.question: How many attempts does A-ProS get?
questions.answer: At most four submissions: Itr_0 is the initial candidate, followed by Itr_1, Itr_2 and Itr_3 after three feedback rounds.
detail: Stop earlier if the judge accepts.
State both the feedback-round budget and total submission budget to prevent off-by-one ambiguity.
questions.caution: Four attempts are not pass@1 and not necessarily equal token compute across workflows.
followups: How would you compare under equal monetary cost?

questions.question: What is the benchmark composition?
questions.answer: 367 problems: 167 ICPC World Finals problems from 2011 to 2024 and 200 Codeforces problems rated 1200 to 1800.
detail: The two subsets have different difficulty distributions and should be reported separately.
LLM-ProS used 166 problems; do not assume the two ICPC collections are identical without an ID-level audit.
questions.caution: The cause of the one-problem dataset difference is not established by the profile.
followups: Why stratify by source and rating?

questions.question: How autonomous was the published workflow?
questions.answer: Solution generation and refinement are model-driven, but the paper describes manual retrieval for some restricted ICPC test diagnostics.
detail: State which parts were automated and which access steps needed human handling.
This matters for reproducibility and practical deployment.
questions.caution: Do not claim a completely human-free pipeline for every ICPC diagnostic step.
followups: Could the method work with verdict-only feedback?

questions.question: Is A-ProS reinforcement learning or RLHF?
questions.answer: No. The evaluated loop changes prompts and context during inference, without updating model parameters.
detail: It can adapt behavior within a task through evidence.
Reinforcement-guided feedback selection is a possible future direction, distinct from what was tested.
questions.caution: Calling every feedback loop reinforcement learning confuses inference with training.
followups: How could an RL policy extend this?

questions.question: What does SQLite logging contribute scientifically?
questions.answer: It links each task, candidate, hint and judge outcome across attempts, enabling trajectory analysis and paired comparisons instead of only final totals.
detail: Structured keys help reconstruct the exact sequence.
Transactional writes and separate run identifiers are useful for reliable collection.
questions.caution: Inspect the actual schema before claiming a particular constraint or recovery policy.
followups: How would you detect duplicate or missing attempts?

questions.question: Why does feedback sometimes make the solution worse?
questions.answer: A revision can fix one issue while creating another, or a critic can give an incorrect diagnosis. Acceptance is not guaranteed to improve monotonically along a single trajectory.
detail: The paper's Sums on Segments example goes Wrong Answer, Time Limit Exceeded, Wrong Answer, Accepted for GPT-4 with DeepSeek.
Track candidate-level regressions as well as eventual success.
questions.caution: A representative trajectory illustrates behavior; it does not estimate its frequency.
followups: How could the loop reject harmful hints?

questions.question: Why are algorithmic tags not disjoint?
questions.answer: A problem may require several techniques, such as graphs and dynamic programming, so it can appear in multiple category counts.
detail: Category totals can exceed the number of distinct problems.
Use task-level paired outcomes when testing workflow differences.
questions.caution: Do not sum overlapping tags into a benchmark size.
followups: How would you compare performance by category?

questions.question: What are the exact ICPC results?
questions.answer: Out of 167 ICPC tasks, GPT-5 workflows start at 39 accepted and finish at 85, 87 and 90. GPT-4 starts at 15 and finishes at 31, 34 and 38.
detail: The critic order for those final counts is Codestral, Llama, DeepSeek.
For GPT-5 with DeepSeek, 39 plus 25 plus 15 plus 11 equals 90.
questions.caution: These counts describe the ICPC subset, not all 367 tasks.
followups: What fraction is 90 out of 167?

questions.question: What are the Codeforces results?
questions.answer: Out of 200 tasks, GPT-5 final counts are 73, 77 and 82; GPT-4 final counts are 42, 47 and 52 for Codestral, Llama and DeepSeek respectively.
detail: The corresponding GPT-5 rates are 36.5%, 38.5% and 41.0%.
Unlike the ICPC table, initial counts differ slightly across critic workflows in this subset.
questions.caution: Preserve each row's own initial baseline when calculating its improvement.
followups: Is the best critic significantly better?

questions.question: Are iteration columns cumulative or incremental?
questions.answer: Tables 6 and 7 report new solves at each iteration. Add the columns through Itr_k to obtain cumulative acceptance by that point.
detail: For GPT-5 with DeepSeek on ICPC: 39, 25, 15, 11 are incremental; 39, 64, 79, 90 are cumulative.
questions.caution: Mixing these definitions can turn 11 new final-round solves into a misleading final total.
followups: How would you plot the trajectory?

questions.question: What did the 47-problem memory study show?
questions.answer: GPT-5 with DeepSeek reached 19 of 47 statefully versus 14 statelessly; GPT-4 reached 12 versus 8. That is a 10.6 and 8.5 percentage-point advantage.
detail: Baselines were 10 and 5 initial solves respectively.
Repeated verdict categories decreased from 41.8% to 11.8% for GPT-5 and 40.8% to 14.2% for GPT-4.
questions.caution: The solve-rate effects are descriptive and statistically inconclusive.
followups: What were the p-values?

questions.question: Was the memory solve-rate result statistically significant?
questions.answer: No. Raw exact McNemar p-values are 0.063 and 0.125, and the reported bootstrap confidence intervals touch zero.
detail: Say the measured direction was promising on this small matched set.
Avoid claiming that the ablation established a statistically conclusive acceptance benefit.
questions.caution: A result just above 0.05 is still not significant at that threshold.
followups: What larger experiment would you run?

questions.question: What does 3.5 times less error repetition mean?
questions.answer: For GPT-5, the reported repetition rate is 41.8% stateless versus 11.8% stateful; their ratio is about 3.5. GPT-4 gives about 2.9.
detail: Repetition means consecutive attempts have the same failure verdict type.
Two wrong answers can have different semantic causes.
questions.caution: Do not equate repeated verdicts with independently identified repeated reasoning mistakes.
followups: What annotation would measure repeated semantic mistakes?

questions.question: What does more than two times greater gains mean?
questions.answer: It compares improvement over the initial baseline. GPT-5 gains 9 stateful solves versus 4 stateless solves, giving 2.25 times the gain; GPT-4 gains 7 versus 3, giving 2.33.
detail: Final GPT-5 counts are 19 versus 14, whose ratio is only 1.36.
Keep gain ratios, final-rate ratios and percentage-point differences separate.
questions.caution: The small ablation's uncertainty still applies to these ratios.
followups: Can you calculate the absolute difference?

questions.question: Is DeepSeek conclusively the best critic?
questions.answer: It has the best observed results in these comparisons, but individual critic-pair differences were not significant after multiplicity correction.
detail: A consistent descriptive ranking is useful to report.
It is weaker evidence than a statistically established universal critic ranking.
questions.caution: Generator-tier differences are stronger in the reported analysis; do not transfer their significance to critic pairs.
followups: How would a routing policy be evaluated?

questions.question: What is verification cost in the tables?
questions.answer: Total judge submissions across all tasks divided by the number of accepted solutions, including submissions spent on tasks that remain unsolved.
detail: It measures judge attempts per solved task.
It is not dollars, token usage or average attempts only among successful tasks.
questions.caution: Read the table caption before comparing cost metrics.
followups: What other costs should be reported?

questions.question: Can you explain critic calibration?
questions.answer: We ask for confidence from 1 to 5, map it to 0.2 to 1.0 and compare that confidence with whether the immediately following revision is accepted.
detail: Expected Calibration Error is a bin-frequency-weighted absolute gap between confidence and observed success.
Confidence concerns an outcome involving both critic and generator.
questions.caution: Acceptance is a proxy for hint utility, not a direct label that the entire diagnosis was correct.
followups: Why is the confidence floor a problem?

questions.question: What did the calibration results imply?
questions.answer: All tested pairings had reported ECE above 0.35. DeepSeek was relatively better calibrated, but none should be trusted just because it expresses confidence.
detail: A 1-to-5 scale cannot express success probabilities below 20%.
These hints arise after failures, so the outcome population is already conditional on difficulty.
questions.caution: Calibration-based routing is proposed future work, not a proven component of A-ProS.
followups: How would you recalibrate a critic?

questions.question: How would you explain ECE with numbers?
questions.answer: If 20 hints all carry confidence 0.8 but only 4 next attempts succeed, that bin has observed success 0.2 and an absolute calibration gap of 0.6.
detail: Weight that gap by the fraction of all hints in the bin, then sum across bins.
This is an illustrative calculation, not a new paper result.
questions.caution: ECE depends on binning and can hide local or subgroup errors.
followups: Would a Brier score add information?

questions.question: Could persistent context simply use more compute?
questions.answer: Yes, retained history can increase input tokens even when submission counts match. An equal-attempt study does not fully control compute or monetary cost.
detail: Compare full history, structured summaries, latest feedback and retrieval under matched token or money budgets.
questions.caution: That is a proposed follow-up; the published result does not settle it.
followups: What is the appropriate budget for deployment?

questions.question: What was the hardest engineering challenge?
questions.answer: A strong answer is maintaining a trustworthy mapping from task and model response to browser submission, delayed verdict and later feedback, while preserving complete trajectories.
detail: Connect the automation to validity: a misattributed verdict invalidates a revision step.
Use a concrete incident you remember rather than inventing a debugging anecdote.
questions.caution: This is a suggested framing based on recorded responsibilities, not a documented incident.
followups: What did you change after a real failure?

questions.question: What are the biggest limitations of A-ProS?
questions.answer: Narrow contest tasks, a small memory ablation, expensive context, uncertain critic reliability and dependence on access to useful execution feedback.
detail: The design also does not isolate the causal benefit of different-model criticism against a same-model control.
Good contest performance does not establish robust repository maintenance.
questions.caution: State limitations with their consequences rather than listing generic threats.
followups: Which one matters most for your PhD work?

questions.question: Would a same-model critic work just as well?
questions.answer: It might. I would add same-model generator-critic controls under the same task, prompt and total budget to isolate whether model diversity contributes beyond role separation.
detail: Include verdict-only self-revision and fresh resampling baselines.
Measure both acceptance and the semantic quality of hints.
questions.caution: This comparison is proposed, not an established A-ProS result.
questions.locator: Proposed control motivated by factorial design
followups: How would you prevent unequal inference budgets?

questions.question: How would you improve memory?
questions.answer: Replace raw history with an evidence ledger of attempted hypotheses, changed code, verdicts and unresolved constraints, then compare it with full context under equal cost.
detail: A summary can reduce context length and make contradictions visible.
It can also lose essential detail, so measure retention errors.
questions.caution: Structured memory is an experiment to run, not a demonstrated improvement.
followups: What would the ablation conditions be?

questions.question: How would you test whether a hint is actually useful?
questions.answer: Hold the task and candidate fixed, randomly assign a real hint, a shuffled hint, verdict-only feedback or no hint, then compare matched revisions.
detail: Blind reviewers can separately label diagnosis accuracy and actionability.
Keep generator sampling and budget comparable.
questions.caution: An immediate accepted revision alone cannot establish that every hint was correct.
followups: Why include a shuffled-hint control?

questions.question: How would you reduce cost without losing reliability?
questions.answer: Test early stopping, compact history and critic escalation under a fixed budget, and report a cost-success frontier instead of only the best accuracy.
detail: Route using validated signals, not uncalibrated self-confidence alone.
Count failed tasks in total spend.
questions.caution: These are proposed policies; their benefit remains to be measured.
questions.locator: Proposed extension from calibration and verification cost
followups: What if a cheap critic gives harmful advice?

questions.question: What happens when judge feedback is sparse?
questions.answer: A verdict-only signal can say a candidate failed without explaining why. I would compare verdict-only, examples and richer diagnostics to quantify feedback requirements.
detail: Let the agent construct its own reproductions under a separate visible-test budget.
Keep hidden evaluation tests inaccessible.
questions.caution: Rich-feedback performance should not be assumed to survive sparse feedback.
followups: How do you distinguish feedback and scoring?

questions.question: What is XLAgent in 30 seconds?
questions.answer: It studies and attempts to repair bugs caused by interactions across Java-TypeScript and Python-Go boundaries, using a navigation graph, localization, contract reasoning and editing in an isolated harness.
detail: Explain the empirical study before the agent: 145 repositories, 86 confirmed fixes, 31 strict fixes.
The headline is a careful account of what structure helps and where evaluation fails.
questions.caution: The manuscript is in preparation, and repair superiority was not established.
followups: What qualifies as a cross-language bug?

questions.question: What is the purpose of XLAgent?
questions.answer: To understand cross-language defects, recover their relationships and test whether that evidence helps an agent localize and repair both sides reliably.
detail: Repository language counts alone are insufficient; the key is the interaction contract.
The study joins mining, program analysis and evaluation of an agent workflow.
questions.caution: The empirical study, graph quality and repair outcomes answer different questions.
followups: Why did you choose these language pairs?

questions.question: What did you personally do in XLAgent?
questions.answer: I carried out the project independently with Md. Fahim Arefin as PI, covering corpus mining, graph tooling, agent infrastructure and evaluation.
detail: Discuss one complete experiment: define eligibility, prepare snapshots, run controlled systems, audit leakage and interpret failures.
Acknowledge supervision and distinguish implementation work from review judgments.
questions.caution: This personal-ownership statement is recorded in the prior research refresher.
followups: Which decision most changed the paper?

questions.question: What is a strict cross-language bug?
questions.answer: A defect whose fix changes non-test source in both languages, with those changes needed together because of how the sides interact.
detail: Adding an endpoint and a client is a feature, not necessarily a repair.
Two independent same-PR fixes or a test-only change on one side do not meet the strict criterion.
questions.caution: Multiple changed languages do not automatically establish a cross-language defect.
followups: Give a positive and a negative example.

questions.question: How did you build the corpus?
questions.answer: Mine 145 repositories, find 1,206 merged PRs changing both languages, filter to 668 candidates, confirm 86 fixes, then retain 31 under strict interaction criteria.
detail: Human review covered early candidates and model-positive labels; judges later reassessed confirmed fixes.
Preserve each denominator because filtering and strict adjudication answer different questions.
questions.caution: This pipeline is not a population prevalence estimate.
followups: What could the filters miss?

questions.question: Why did the corpus shrink from 86 to 31?
questions.answer: Stricter review required non-test changes in both languages and evidence that their interaction made both changes necessary. Many broad candidates failed that test.
detail: Exclusions included one-language source fixes, independent or cosmetic changes and non-defect changes.
The reduction narrows the claim to a more defensible construct.
questions.caution: Use current strict-set results, not the superseded 86-fix analysis.
followups: Did the new definition change the conclusions?

questions.question: Why select Java-TypeScript and Python-Go?
questions.answer: They cover common backend/frontend or mobile-bridge patterns and infrastructure/ML client-service patterns, while exposing different interface mechanisms.
detail: Java-TypeScript includes many native-bridge fixes; Python-Go includes REST and gRPC cases.
The pairs let us see whether one tool generalizes across boundary kinds.
questions.caution: They are a purposive sample, not representative of every language combination.
followups: Why not Python-Java or C++?

questions.question: What repository filters did you use?
questions.answer: The mining used activity, age, stars, CI and license criteria, excluded forks and non-project examples, and required meaningful bytes from both languages.
detail: The paper records at least 500 stars, a recent push and six-month age, with a smaller second-language threshold for Python-Go.
Those choices improve tractability but bias the sample toward established projects.
questions.caution: The resulting corpus excludes much private and small-project software.
followups: How would you test robustness to those filters?

questions.question: What is the largest strict root-cause category?
questions.answer: Contract and schema mismatches: 11 of 31 strict fixes, about 35%.
detail: Examples include incompatible fields, routes, enums or message shapes.
A root cause describes why behavior broke; a boundary describes how components communicate.
questions.caution: Do not use the older 27-of-86 count for the strict set.
followups: How is that different from a boundary category?

questions.question: Which boundaries dominate?
questions.answer: Native bridges account for 13 strict fixes, REST 6, gRPC 4, shared files 2, subprocesses 2 and other boundaries 4.
detail: All native-bridge and subprocess fixes are Java-TypeScript; all gRPC and shared-file fixes are Python-Go.
A language pair's boundary mix determines what a graph extractor can cover.
questions.caution: These are corpus counts, not ecosystem frequencies.
followups: Why does graph coverage differ between pairs?

questions.question: How reliable are the labels?
questions.answer: Inclusion required substantial interpretation. Judges agreed more on whether both languages changed than on whether the changes depended on each other.
detail: The draft reports kappa 0.97 on two-language non-test changes but 0.34 on interdependence in the all-fix review.
Author review and recorded rationales expose disagreement.
questions.caution: Agreement is not ground truth, and LLM judges can share biases.
followups: How would you add independent expert review?

questions.question: Can 31 divided by 1206 estimate prevalence?
questions.answer: No. The pipeline uses keyword filtering, selective review and unreviewed model-negative candidates. The retained fraction reflects this process, not all cross-language bugs in an ecosystem.
detail: Report the selection funnel transparently.
A prevalence study would need representative sampling and audits of rejected cases.
questions.caution: Do not interpret the confirmation ratio as a general defect rate.
followups: How would you estimate missed positives?

questions.question: What was the false-negative concern in mining?
questions.answer: The model's negative labels were not all manually checked, so relevant fixes may have been missed before the strict review.
detail: Review a random stratified sample of negatives and estimate recall with uncertainty.
The draft reports a later classifier check against the first 100 manually reviewed cases.
questions.caution: Reviewing every positive removes some false positives, not false negatives.
followups: Why does precision alone not validate the corpus?

questions.question: Give a concrete cross-language example.
questions.answer: In the kagent motivating case, model options cross from a Go-side service into a Python client. Fixing only representation on one side can leave the other side interpreting them incorrectly.
detail: Trace producer, serialized payload, receiving API and expected types.
The repair results show that Go-only hidden tests can accept a patch while Python behavior remains wrong.
questions.caution: Use the manuscript's actual case; invented endpoint names would only be an illustration.
followups: Why can the hidden tests miss the other side?

questions.question: What is the cross-language graph?
questions.answer: It combines per-language symbols and references from SCIP with explicit edges across REST, headers, payloads, enums, signals and protobuf-mediated RPCs.
detail: Each boundary edge records the mediator that justifies the connection.
Tree-sitter adds syntax ranges and supports extraction where semantic indexing is incomplete.
questions.caution: It is a dependency/navigation graph, not a sound complete call graph for all dynamic behavior.
followups: How are routes matched?

questions.question: What is SCIP used for?
questions.answer: SCIP provides structured symbols and references inside each language, giving stable entities that cross-language edges can connect.
detail: Function-body ranges from tree-sitter help attribute references to containing functions.
Java build failures may require a definitions-only fallback.
questions.caution: Definitions-only fallback loses semantic reference information.
followups: How does tree-sitter complement SCIP?

questions.question: Why use tree-sitter too?
questions.answer: It supplies syntax structure and body ranges useful for locating definitions and extracting interface patterns when symbol indexes alone are insufficient.
detail: It is especially useful for route literals, payload declarations and fallback definitions.
A parser recognizes syntax; it does not automatically resolve runtime dispatch.
questions.caution: Do not equate AST availability with complete semantic understanding.
questions.locator: Methodology, per-language symbols and boundary edges
followups: What dynamic cases remain unresolved?

questions.question: How do you connect REST clients and handlers?
questions.answer: Extract HTTP methods and normalized route templates, fold supported constant URL expressions, then match clients to handlers through the mediator.
detail: Supported expressions include concatenation, template literals, f-strings and formatted strings.
Ambiguous matches and unresolved symbols should remain visible rather than becoming unqualified edges.
questions.caution: Dynamic routing, proxies and conditional configuration can defeat static matching.
followups: How would you handle a reverse proxy?

questions.question: How do gRPC edges work?
questions.answer: Proto definitions become a shared indexed mediator, linking a client stub call to the RPC method and then to its server implementation.
detail: Message types and service definitions create more explicit cross-language contracts than arbitrary strings.
That helps explain strong precision for sampled gRPC edges.
questions.caution: Strong sampled precision does not establish complete recall.
followups: Why can gRPC be easier than HTTP headers?

questions.question: How big is the graph?
questions.answer: The draft reports 9,605 boundary edges across the indexed snapshots, including 8,565 cross-language edges and 1,040 same-language REST route edges.
detail: This distinction matters when quoting precision, which was estimated for the cross-language population.
Most cross-language edges are gRPC.
questions.caution: Do not imply every one of the 9,605 edges was manually validated.
followups: What does 91.1% apply to?

questions.question: What does the 91% precision estimate mean?
questions.answer: A stratified labeled sample estimates that 91.1% of the 8,565 cross-language edges are directly correct, or 94.3% if indirect links count.
detail: Stratum weights matter because gRPC dominates the population and is easier than several other edge types.
The strict reported interval is broad, about 77% to 93%.
questions.caution: This is estimated precision, not recall, and excludes same-language route edges.
followups: Why not use raw sample accuracy?

questions.question: What graph coverage did you obtain?
questions.answer: It connected both halves for 11 of 12 strict fixes at the modeled REST, gRPC and shared-file boundaries. Across all indexed strict fixes it connected 13 of 30.
detail: The difference exposes unsupported native bridges and subprocesses.
State the in-scope denominator whenever using the 11-of-12 result.
questions.caution: 11 of 12 is not coverage of all 31 strict fixes.
followups: Which missing boundary would you implement first?

questions.question: What is a graph-connected bug?
questions.answer: Within the stated hop limit, graph entities in developer-changed files on each side are linked through a boundary edge, shared schema or common boundary.
detail: This is a reference-fix-based coverage criterion.
It measures recoverable relationships relative to known fixes, not whether an agent can discover a new bug unaided.
questions.caution: Gold-guided coverage should not be presented as deployment-time end-to-end recall.
followups: How does indexing use the reference fix?

questions.question: Was graph construction gold-guided?
questions.answer: Yes. Modules containing developer-changed non-test files were chosen for indexing, which uses information unavailable for a new unseen issue.
detail: This makes graph quality easier to study at manageable cost but can reveal relevant module scope.
A deployment study would index independently of the fix.
questions.caution: This is an important limitation even though the graph did not improve localization.
followups: What would a fair deployment simulation change?

questions.question: What is the agent pipeline?
questions.answer: A read-only localizer finds relevant sites; contract reasoning summarizes boundary evidence; an editor patches; a validation gate checks new basic errors; visible tests can trigger another round.
detail: The hidden scoring tests remain outside that loop.
The agent uses a shell-accessible navigation command with compact path-and-line outputs.
questions.caution: A diagram describes implementation, not evidence that each component improves outcomes.
followups: What does the gate guarantee?

questions.question: Why separate localization from editing?
questions.answer: It creates an explicit read-only evidence-gathering phase and a structured handoff before modifications, which makes the process easier to inspect.
detail: A matched single-agent control tests whether two roles matter beyond tools, budgets and prompts.
questions.caution: The current five-bug evidence cannot attribute two-sided edits to the split alone.
followups: Did the ablation establish a benefit?

questions.question: What does contract reasoning do?
questions.answer: Group edges by route, header, RPC or payload, check deterministic mismatches and ask a model for up to three fix hypotheses grounded in those contracts.
detail: Checks include unmatched routes, one-sided fields or enum members and RPC callers without a server.
Skip the step when no relevant contract is found.
questions.caution: A flagged difference is not automatically a bug; legitimate asymmetry exists.
followups: How would you measure hypothesis grounding?

questions.question: What does the validation gate check?
questions.answer: Syntax, compilation and selected lint or vet checks on touched code, comparing against the unpatched snapshot so pre-existing errors are not blamed on the patch.
detail: Missing dependencies can cause a check to be skipped and recorded.
A first one-sided submission may be returned for reconsideration if localization identified both sides.
questions.caution: Passing the gate does not prove semantic correctness; a deliberate one-sided patch can still be submitted.
followups: Why compare with the original snapshot?

questions.question: How is feedback routed?
questions.answer: Visible repository tests run after gate acceptance. New failures on one side send investigation to that side; failures on both sides direct attention toward the interaction contract.
detail: Compare with baseline tests to identify newly introduced failures.
Hidden fail-to-pass scoring tests are not used as agent feedback.
questions.caution: Routing embodies a heuristic and did not establish a measurable repair gain in the ablation.
followups: What if the test cannot run?

questions.question: Did the graph improve localization?
questions.answer: No measurable improvement was found. On 12 strict localization bugs, the shell-only localizer found both developer-file sides in every run.
detail: Across three replicates, mean file-level counts were 10.7 for XL navigation, 11.7 for graph without boundary edges and 12.0 for shell.
Shared names made ordinary search effective.
questions.caution: A useful graph representation is not the same as a useful intervention for this agent.
followups: Why might the benchmark hide a graph benefit?

questions.question: Why could grep perform as well as the graph?
questions.answer: Many boundaries are mediated by a shared route, type, enum or configuration string. Searching that name across languages can reveal the same endpoints.
detail: The graph often formalizes the same lexical relation.
Harder cases with indirection or mismatched names may be more informative, but need separate evaluation.
questions.caution: Do not claim the graph is universally useless from this small task set.
followups: What would be a genuinely graph-dependent task?

questions.question: How many executable repair bugs were there?
questions.answer: Five strict executable bugs from three repositories, all Python-Go, with three runs per configuration.
detail: Seven configurations give 105 usable repair/ablation runs in the contemporaneous batch.
Localization uses 12 bugs and corpus analysis uses 31; these are separate populations.
questions.caution: Five tasks sharply limit inference and generalization.
followups: Why were Java-TypeScript bugs absent from repair?

questions.question: What are the main repair results?
questions.answer: XLAgent edited developer-changed files in both languages on an average 4.0 of 5 bugs, versus 2.7 for baseline and 3.0 for the matched single agent.
detail: Only kagent 1245 was ever resolved by hidden tests.
XLAgent resolved it in two of three runs, baseline in all three.
questions.caution: More two-sided edits did not establish higher repair correctness.
followups: Is editing both sides itself success?

questions.question: What is the difference between two-sided and correct?
questions.answer: Two-sided means the patch touches a counted source file in each language. Correctness requires the intended behavior to work, including the contract connecting those sides.
detail: A patch can modify both relevant files incorrectly.
A valid alternative fix could also differ from the developers' chosen file set.
questions.caution: The metric describes patch shape and reference overlap, not complete behavior.
followups: Can a valid repair be one-sided?

questions.question: What is cross-language blindness?
questions.answer: In this paper it means changing non-test code in only one language, despite a strict task whose reference fix changes both sides.
detail: The metric helps diagnose ignoring an interaction partner.
A one-sided count is a heuristic signal; it does not independently prove the candidate is invalid.
questions.caution: The operational definition is narrower than every possible meaning of blindness.
followups: How does the gate handle a deliberate one-sided fix?

questions.question: Why are hidden tests not definitive here?
questions.answer: They exercise one language, so passing can miss a defect on the other side. Three suites also depend on developer-introduced names and can reject alternate valid repairs.
detail: Thus both false success and false failure are plausible and observed in the analysis.
Use side-specific assessment and behavior-based tests as complementary evidence.
questions.caution: This does not justify dismissing every failed repair as an oracle problem.
followups: What independent evidence would you require?

questions.question: What is implementation-coupled testing?
questions.answer: A test assumes an internal helper, private member or new identifier used by the reference patch, even when the user-visible requirement allows other implementations.
detail: In this repair set, 3 of 5 suites have such assumptions.
A repair using another valid internal design can fail to compile against the overlaid tests.
questions.caution: Externally specified API names can be legitimate requirements; coupling needs case-specific evidence.
followups: How would you rewrite the oracle?

questions.question: Did the judges validate repair superiority?
questions.answer: No. The LLM judges counted 3 of 15 XLAgent patches fully correct versus 4 baseline patches; the author pass was stricter, finding 0 versus 1.
detail: The author disagreed substantially with model judgments.
Report both assessments and their limitations rather than choosing the favorable one.
questions.caution: Judge consensus is an imperfect measurement, not ground truth.
followups: What does disagreement reveal?

questions.question: What did the ablations show?
questions.answer: Removing boundary edges, contracts, feedback or navigation did not measurably change repairs, and two-sided edits persisted across conditions.
detail: The matched single agent came close.
On five bugs we cannot attribute a gain to a particular component or to the split into two agents.
questions.caution: Null evidence here is not proof of equal performance in all settings.
followups: What larger controlled experiment is needed?

questions.question: Why add a matched single agent?
questions.answer: A stock baseline differs in several ways. The matched control keeps more of the workflow machinery and budget while combining localization and editing in one agent.
detail: It tests whether the role split matters beyond shared prompts, gate and feedback.
Its 3.0-of-5 two-sided-file count is close to XLAgent's 4.0.
questions.caution: The control still differs in the availability of a localization report and related checks.
followups: What residual confounds remain?

questions.question: Why not report a significance win on five bugs?
questions.answer: A five-task paired sign test has very low resolution: even all five favoring one system gives a minimum two-sided p-value of 0.0625.
detail: The draft therefore reports per-bug outcomes for repair.
More stochastic runs improve within-task estimates but do not create more independent bug tasks.
questions.caution: Treating 15 patches as 15 independent bugs would overstate effective sample size.
followups: What sample size would support your hypothesis?

questions.question: Why rerun all repair conditions in one batch?
questions.answer: The provider's model behind an alias changed during earlier experiments. A single contemporaneous batch with the same fingerprint reduces version drift as a confound.
detail: The strict-corpus batch has 105 usable runs on one backend version.
Preserve reported response identities, not just the requested alias.
questions.caution: This controls one source of variation, not all stochastic or temporal effects.
questions.locator: Setup, model version and batch protocol
followups: What if the provider does not expose fingerprints?

questions.question: How much did XLAgent cost?
questions.answer: The reported strict repair table gives about $0.15 per full-system run and $0.07 per baseline run under the study's provider pricing.
detail: The 105-run strict batch is recorded as $11.79 in project status.
This is model API spend, not total engineering, indexing or infrastructure cost.
questions.caution: Historical prices are not a current cost estimate or a promise for another model.
questions.locator: RQ4 cost table; 20 October batch status
followups: How would you compare success under a fixed budget?

questions.question: What are the limits of the issue statements?
questions.answer: The strict localization set uses linked-issue material; 19 of 31 corpus statements otherwise came from PR descriptions that can disclose the fix. Repair tasks use short PR titles without linked issues.
detail: Sparse titles can omit required semantics.
Issue-only protocols reduce some solution leakage but can also make the task underspecified.
questions.caution: Do not assume every title supplies a complete specification.
followups: How would you build realistic issue reports?

questions.question: What leakage did you discover?
questions.answer: Before isolation, agents could read developer fixes through Git history, local caches or network access. The record reports this in 13 of 16 baseline runs.
detail: A later graph-tool checkout leak exposed uncommitted fixed source in eight runs and required reruns.
The lesson is to inspect every surface the tools can read.
questions.caution: This is runtime solution leakage, separate from possible pretraining contamination.
followups: What safeguards did you implement?

questions.question: How did you prevent runtime leakage?
questions.answer: Run each agent on a single-commit pre-fix snapshot with no remote, deny network and outside-file access, isolate scoring artifacts and audit trajectories and tool outputs.
detail: Test known escape attempts before paid batches.
Graph-tool working copies need cleanliness and snapshot checks too.
questions.caution: No audit flag means no detected violation under that audit, not a formal proof of total isolation.
followups: Why was removing the remote insufficient?

questions.question: Why was the graph-tool checkout leak subtle?
questions.answer: The agent's own workspace could be clean while a separate tool server read another checkout containing uncommitted developer fixes.
detail: Tools are part of the evidence boundary.
Validate what the server reads, not just what the agent's shell sees.
questions.caution: Fixing shell isolation alone would not address this channel.
followups: How would you test tool isolation automatically?

questions.question: How did you handle contaminated results?
questions.answer: Exclude affected runs, repair the leak, rerun the conditions and retain an audit trail of discarded batches and replacement results.
detail: The earlier broad-set resolved score dropped after reruns.
Use the current strict-set numbers in interviews instead of mixing batches.
questions.caution: Do not selectively retain a favorable exposed run because it looks plausible.
questions.locator: Isolation protocol; batch registry; results revisions
followups: What would you include in a release archive?

questions.question: What is an oracle-policy sanity test?
questions.answer: A scripted reference-fix policy exercises the sandbox, gate, feedback and scorer to check that the environment can recognize the known fix before agent evaluation.
detail: It is a harness validation run with privileged solution access.
An escape-attempt policy separately checks the isolation boundary.
questions.caution: Oracle policies are not agent performance results and must not be pooled with them.
followups: What if the reference fix does not pass?

questions.question: What would you say if asked whether the project failed?
questions.answer: The intended repair advantage was not established, but the study produced a stricter corpus, measured graph limits, controlled baselines and concrete evidence about leakage and unsuitable oracles.
detail: Explain what the hypothesis predicted, what the data contradicted and what you changed.
The value is an accurate account of the problem, not a forced positive result.
questions.caution: Keep the practical repair limitations explicit.
followups: What is the next falsifiable hypothesis?

questions.question: What remains unfinished?
questions.answer: The manuscript is in preparation; venue and final release decisions need author coordination. Broader executable coverage and stronger behavior-based evaluation remain research needs.
detail: The draft is formatted toward MSR 2027 and the application record says preparation for that submission.
Do not call it submitted or accepted without an updated record.
questions.caution: Project status contains superseded sections; use the latest strict revision for numbers.
questions.locator: Manuscript main.tex; current application research record
followups: What would you prioritize before submission?

questions.question: What is your strongest takeaway from XLAgent?
questions.answer: Better-looking structure and more two-sided edits are insufficient. We need an isolated, valid measurement process that can tell whether the cross-language behavior was repaired.
detail: A graph can be precise without adding localization value.
A hidden suite can pass while one side remains wrong.
questions.caution: Each conclusion is bounded by the tested tasks and tools.
followups: How would that shape your PhD research?

questions.question: Why do you want a PhD?
questions.answer: I want to learn how to formulate and test research questions about reliable software agents, beyond building a system that merely appears to work. My projects made evaluation quality and cross-component reasoning central interests.
detail: Connect LLM-ProS measurement, A-ProS feedback and XLAgent evaluation limits.
Explain the kind of mentorship and methodological depth you seek.
questions.caution: Personalize the motivation; this is suggested practice language.
followups: Why now?
Why this laboratory?

questions.question: What is your proposed PhD topic?
questions.answer: A strong starting direction is reliable diagnosis and repair of interacting software components, especially cross-language contracts, with evidence that supports behavioral correctness.
detail: One tractable question is whether contract-focused reproductions improve correctness under matched budgets.
Another is how to build oracles that accept valid alternative repairs and check both sides.
questions.caution: Present a focused starting agenda and flexibility, not a guaranteed dissertation result.
questions.locator: Proposed direction from XLAgent and A-ProS
followups: What is your first experiment?

questions.question: What would your first PhD experiment be?
questions.answer: Start with a small, independently validated set of interaction bugs and compare shell search, static contract evidence and generated boundary tests under matched model and budget conditions.
detail: Make the primary outcome behavior on both sides, not file overlap.
Predefine exclusions, failure categories and the condition that would refute the hypothesis.
questions.caution: First validate the environment and oracle before spending on many agent runs.
followups: What would a negative result tell you?

questions.question: What is a falsifiable research hypothesis for you?
questions.answer: Contract-grounded reproductions improve independently assessed cross-boundary behavior compared with equally budgeted unstructured feedback on the same bugs.
detail: Specify the population, control, intervention, metric and analysis before running.
If behavior does not improve, investigate evidence quality rather than redefining success as more edits.
questions.caution: This is a proposed hypothesis, not an XLAgent finding.
followups: What are the confounders?

questions.question: What would you work on if graphs keep showing null effects?
questions.answer: Study where agents lack information rather than adding structure by default: ambiguous contracts, indirect boundaries, incomplete reproductions and weak evaluation oracles.
detail: A stratified dataset can test whether graph value depends on boundary type or lexical overlap.
A robust null result can redirect the method.
questions.caution: Do not keep increasing graph complexity without a measurable target.
followups: How do you choose between tool and benchmark work?

questions.question: What is novel about the direction?
questions.answer: A plausible contribution combines independently validated interaction tasks, behavior-based cross-boundary oracles and controlled evidence interventions. I would verify novelty through a focused literature review with the advisor.
detail: Explain the gap operationally: current patch-shape measures and one-sided tests cannot establish a complete interaction repair.
questions.caution: Do not claim to be the first without a systematic prior-work check.
followups: What existing systems are closest?

questions.question: How do you choose a research question?
questions.answer: Start from a reproducible failure, ask what current evidence cannot distinguish, then design the cheapest experiment that separates competing explanations.
detail: In XLAgent, two-sided edits and passing one-sided tests prompted different explanations of success.
Favor a question whose negative result would still be informative.
questions.caution: Give a specific project example rather than a general slogan.
followups: How do you decide to stop an experiment?

questions.question: How would you measure research progress in year one?
questions.answer: Establish a reproducible task set, trustworthy baseline and one carefully controlled experiment, then write what the evidence supports and revise the agenda with the advisor.
detail: Track artifact quality, answered questions and remaining uncertainty alongside publication plans.
Set milestones with explicit exit criteria.
questions.caution: Avoid promising a specific acceptance or arbitrary benchmark win.
followups: What if reproduction takes longer than expected?

questions.question: Why this professor or lab?
questions.answer: Connect one specific verified research problem from the lab to a failure mode or method you understand from your own work, then explain what you hope to learn and contribute.
detail: Prepare: paper claim, method, limitation and a concrete follow-up question.
Use the interview to test mutual fit.
questions.caution: This answer must be customized after reading that lab's current work.
followups: Which of their recent papers interests you?

questions.question: Are you open to changing topics?
questions.answer: Yes. My anchor is reliable evidence for software-agent behavior, and I can adapt the task or technique to the advisor's expertise and what experiments reveal.
detail: Distinguish a durable question from a preferred tool such as graphs or multiple agents.
Name one adjacent area you would explore.
questions.caution: Flexibility should still come with a concrete initial research interest.
followups: What adjacent topics are attractive?

questions.question: Why pursue research instead of only industry engineering?
questions.answer: Engineering taught me to build and maintain systems; research lets me test general explanations for why methods work or fail and produce evidence others can reuse.
detail: Connect an actual engineering responsibility to a research question.
A PhD is also sustained work under uncertainty and critique, which these projects helped me experience.
questions.caution: Do not dismiss industry work or invent career promises.
followups: How does your current job help research?

questions.question: What is your long-term goal?
questions.answer: A defensible answer is to develop rigorous methods and reusable evaluation infrastructure for reliable software agents, in a research role where I can keep asking and testing such questions.
detail: If academia or industry research is your actual preference, say so and explain why.
Tie the goal to impact on developers and reproducible knowledge.
questions.caution: The available records do not fix one permanent career choice; personalize this.
followups: What impact would make the work worthwhile?

questions.question: How would you handle a negative result?
questions.answer: Check the implementation and measurement, report the result at the level the design supports, then test whether the theory, intervention or task distribution needs revision.
detail: XLAgent's graph result is a concrete example: useful recovered relationships did not translate into localization improvement.
Preserve the null result rather than hiding it in an appendix.
questions.caution: A non-significant result is not automatically proof of equivalence.
followups: What evidence would change your mind?

questions.question: How would you address a low sample size?
questions.answer: Expand independent tasks and repositories, preserve paired conditions and stratify by boundary and difficulty. More random seeds alone do not fix a five-task population.
detail: Use a pilot to estimate variance and choose an effect size of practical interest.
Report uncertainty and avoid post-hoc significance hunting.
questions.caution: A formal sample-size plan depends on the endpoint and task dependence.
followups: What counts as an independent observation?

questions.question: How do you avoid overfitting a benchmark?
questions.answer: Freeze evaluation tasks and criteria, keep development cases separate, disclose model access and test use, and replicate on new repositories or later time windows.
detail: Repeated inspection of failing evaluation cases can turn a test set into a development set.
Record what was known when designing the method.
questions.caution: A held-out split is only useful if the information boundary is enforced.
followups: What is leakage through manual development?

questions.question: How would you explain a limitation without weakening your case?
questions.answer: State the evidence, its limit and the next experiment it motivates. For example: five repair bugs show a patch-shape pattern but cannot establish general correctness improvement.
detail: Specific limitations show that you know what the experiment actually measured.
Pair the limitation with a concrete remedy.
questions.caution: Do not replace unsupported certainty with a vague list of every conceivable threat.
followups: Which limitation is most serious?

questions.question: What if the advisor disagrees with your interpretation?
questions.answer: Ask which assumption or evidence differs, reproduce the comparison together, and design a test that could distinguish the interpretations.
detail: Separate the shared facts from causal explanations and priorities.
Document the decision and what would reopen it.
questions.caution: Supply a real example if asked; do not invent a conflict.
followups: How do you take critical feedback?

questions.question: How do you read a paper efficiently?
questions.answer: Identify the claim, unit of analysis, comparison, metric and strongest limitation, then trace one result back to the protocol and artifacts.
detail: Prepare a one-minute explanation and one unanswered methodological question.
Check whether evidence is observational, controlled or anecdotal.
questions.caution: Reading an abstract alone is not enough for a detailed criticism.
followups: What would you ask the authors?

questions.question: How would you prioritize with limited compute?
questions.answer: Validate the harness, run a small pilot, eliminate irrelevant conditions, and spend on matched comparisons that answer the core question.
detail: Archive everything so failures still teach something.
Decide stopping criteria before observing favorable results.
questions.caution: Total research cost includes setup and review effort, not only API tokens.
followups: What would you stop doing?

questions.question: What makes your work reproducible?
questions.answer: Reproducibility needs exact artifacts, environments, model-response records, scoring rules and a clear boundary between visible feedback and hidden evaluation.
detail: Separate rerunning analysis from regenerating identical model outputs, which may be impossible for a changing API.
A trajectory archive still lets others audit the observed evidence.
questions.caution: Say what is actually available before promising a complete one-command reproduction.
followups: What if an API model disappears?

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer: I am Md Sifat Hossain, a University of Dhaka CSE graduate and software engineer at Therap BD Ltd. My research has progressed from benchmarking LLM code generation to feedback-driven programming and cross-language debugging.
detail: Briefly connect LLM-ProS, A-ProS and current XLAgent work.
Close with your interest in rigorous evaluation and reliable software agents.
questions.caution: Keep this to roughly one minute and adapt it to the lab.
followups: What do you want to research next?

questions.question: What is the thread connecting all three projects?
questions.answer: They ask how to obtain reliable evidence for automated programming: measure first-attempt capability, study feedback-based improvement, then evaluate repair across interacting components.
detail: The recurring challenge is attributing success or failure correctly.
Each project made the next setting and its limits more visible.
questions.caution: This is a synthesis of the trajectory, not a claim that the studies share the same controlled dataset.
followups: What changed in your thinking?

questions.question: What are you working on currently?
questions.answer: My current research project is XLAgent, a manuscript in preparation on cross-language localization and repair. The latest evidence emphasizes strict corpus definition, null graph-localization effects and limitations of repair evaluation.
detail: Mention engineering work at Therap separately if the interviewer asks about employment.
State the revision date when using experimental numbers.
questions.caution: Do not refer to A-ProS as ongoing if discussing its publication status.
followups: What is the next step?

questions.question: How does your software engineering experience help?
questions.answer: At Therap I work with a Java-based EHR SaaS stack and practical maintenance constraints. That makes interface consistency, reproducibility and safe changes concrete rather than abstract concerns.
detail: Mention Java, Spring, Hibernate and the surrounding web/database stack if relevant.
Connect experience to cross-component reasoning without disclosing employer data.
questions.caution: The research benchmark uses public repositories, not private production data.
followups: Can you give a public technical example?

questions.question: What did your RLHF work teach you?
questions.answer: I worked on code and reasoning annotation and led a ten-person pod, which exposed me to rubric quality, disagreement and consistency in evaluation.
detail: Connect annotation practice to critically assessing LLM judges and reward proxies.
Distinguish this experience from training models in A-ProS.
questions.caution: Do not claim ownership of a proprietary training algorithm or measured model gains absent from the record.
followups: How would you design an annotation rubric?

questions.question: How would you discuss your academic record?
questions.answer: State the recorded CGPA accurately, then connect your readiness to concrete research, implementation and problem-solving evidence. Acknowledge areas where further coursework would help.
detail: CGPA is 3.13 out of 4.00, BSc completed February 2025.
If personal context matters, explain it in your own words only as much as you want.
questions.caution: No invented GPA recovery trend or undisclosed personal narrative is included here.
followups: Which courses prepared you best?

questions.question: How do you describe your publication venues accurately?
questions.answer: LLM-ProS appeared at the LLM4Code workshop co-located with ICSE 2025; A-ProS is recorded as ACM TOSEM 2026; XLAgent remains in preparation.
detail: Use full titles when asked and distinguish workshop, journal and draft.
Equal contribution applies to A-ProS with Anika Tabassum.
questions.caution: Do not call the workshop paper an ICSE main-track paper.
followups: What was your contribution to each?

questions.question: What research skills can you bring immediately?
